The Compensation for Disturbauce ffreland• Bill h., after much contention, passed the House of COOlllO9ll. and been remitted to the Upper Chamber I for adoption or rejection by the Poem. The proceed• inire in the Cononotie have been marked by the moat perveive ...ruction. To a noan the Conservatives j have fought e.ly, oft, and late against the Bill. A ; motion of the Irish p.ty, in the hope of oblaimiug greater couventione than the Bill granted for all parts of Ireland, resorted to tactic of obstruction even more! detertniuedly than they did when the Coneermtivm were in office, and who were most loud in their • oompleints at the hindrance ea.ed to the pro- em.. of legiebtive work. The Whig motion , of the Liberal party, many of whom are as excl..° as the most confirmed Trice, have joined the Tori. and the disaffected Irish repreeentativee in up on- ing the Government. There been been in connection with the Bill a end waste of time is, the Gemmel., and a coneequent hindrance to the pro. gives of other work which the Government had ehaped out for the cession. Argument*, thrashed thread- bare over and over again, have been reiterated day after day in a way that would dietrace • village debating elub and the opponents to . the Government measure have simply played the part of the dog in the manger. By their twaddling they ; sought to emu.° thenteelvee for not doing anything peones!, and for preventing everybody else frees doing eerviceable work. Their wheme use to I drive the Government to make the Bill an " innocent" for shiughter as the time for closing the mission drew nigh. Mr. Glidstone, however, disabused their minds of the idea that the Bill would be relegated to the shelf, though they might pursue their keno. obstruction. He put down hie foot firmly with the intimation that if no work wam to be done there would be no holiday, nut no doubt this had a telling effect upon the Hews. During the debates vehich have taken place much has been said about property having its duties u.s well as ite rights. Unhappily berme the Herring Pend" the rights and duties of landlordism have hitherto had a peculiar blending. We, on this side of the Channel, knowing little of, and aging lees for, the diflioultire under which our Inch fellow eubjecte have had to litho., have been ever ready, iu ne.on and out of mason, to condemn their discmtentedness and perversity. This has ariften in a peat measure from the ignorance that exists as to the d,fference between the . situstioa of the En3lish farmer and that of the Irish ;1 farmer. If an Euglish farmer mime hie voice about the Justice of companiation for unexh nutted improve.- mentii he has made in the land he oocupies there are few emeible people who will meet his contentions . with ridicule. But let an Irishman talk in the eame strain, and his complaint. are ignored as '"ohirney sal botheration." T.n England, when o farmer takes a • holding, he tomely finds erected upon some part of the farm a reeidenee, and outintil din. for the housing of hi* livestock and for the storege of tha produce of his fields and if he improme the propety he rental to a degree beyond which he has not had the full advantage of, he is entitled to consideration in respect of the imprevemente then are meohausted. In Ireland the land is for the moat pest divided into imall biddies., and the tenants of these holdirma have, in the majority of C6llO , not only had to convert their little farms from mere wilds into well cultivated plot., but they have had to erect upon their holdings the requieite farm buildinge, plaes which, in England, are amenity provided ; by the owners of the soil. Indeed he has lied to de everything that the landlord zed tenant perform seemlier on this aide of the Chanael. Beige the passing a the Land Act of 1870 it voun within the power af the landLeird, the moment his tenant had put a wildemess ineo•etate of cultivate., and had erected npon it the ammaary buildings foe farming, to turn him out of hit holding, without the slight°. compensation. By that Act the farmer 1•114 given a right to claim compensation for the skill and capital he had inwested and had not fully enjoyed the advantage of. Still. under that Act, it is possible for a greedy landlord, eubjeet only to the lose of a year'e rent, to mion his lmds with their improvements, and to turn his tenants and their Bondisn into tee highway. 'thin is what has been done in Irelarsi by landlords during the last few years. A Urge army of emutu bul.y baa been employed at the expense of the oountsy in makitig evictiont where the ten.ta could not, by reason of the Who° of the crops, pay their rents. The evideem adduced he Mr. Gladstone that aome thoumude of persons been been evicted during the last Fix months, and that "thy unnober of evic- tions h. Motorised five times as oomparel with three yea:sagain sufficiently striking proof that there must be much misery and heert-burning in Irel.d. It is to allay or prevent much of this misery that the Compensation Bill of the Government has been lorougbt nod premed forward in the face of • strong tactic.. "PPmition. The Opposition have pleaded that the Bill prov'eles for the robbery of the landlords of their This it certainly doe,. but the rights it robe

The time ha mine when land- ' lords are to be taught that it is posible for somebody beeide the owners of broad esree to have • reeted in. tereat in the soil, and that the earth was not created simply fer landlord,. A singular exemplification of this truism, though an antusing illustration of the mistakes that may arise from the c invenied situation of two such houses as Defoe alludes to, occurred the other Sunday evening in St. Helens. A policeman found a man belalwaring a public- house door with his fist, and the officer naturally en- , iletvoured to ascertain from him what his intentions were as to his subsequent proceedings that night. It turned out that the man, who was more than " half Peas over," fancied , that he was at a sanctuary door, and withed to tempgrarily transfer his devotions from the shrine of Bacchus to the In- dependent Chapel. Whether or not the spirit was willing. I will not say, but evidently the flesh was weak as he hail wandered to the public house door in mistake for the chapel door, because of their close proximity. RUNCORN AND SUNDAY TRAVELLING.

Sir,—Our friend Fiances" will get himself disliked in thee Paribmical place, if he persists in advocating the running of trains on the Sabbath-day from the Runcorn Msgr., The town of Runcorn, which lay buried for eta many years like a second Pompeii, was only rescued from what promised to become an eternal oblivion by the con- ed:simian of the splendid bridge over the Mersey and the sudden blase of plablicity which burst upon the place Seemed almost bm much for its unsophisticated inhatiitants, whom privacy had been so rudely broken in upon by the iron horse. `. Fleeces " rereMs to forget that for years and yearn Runcorn had been cantent to remain in a most obscure corner —"art of rot do soo—with but one way in and the earns any out, and therefore out of the " swiin entirely, as far ascommunication with the outside world wan con- cerned. If what Shakespere soya be true, that ° home keeping yooth have ever homely wits," how true it must be of a community which keeps Reel, aloof from the busy world outside Re one narrow limits. Having then so recently emerged from the cramping influences of such a * contracted sphere of existence, It cannot be expected that we ohould take our place among the foremost of the rising municipalities an easily as if we were "to the manner born.' I would, therefore, beg "Flame "to moderate his aml about Sunday railway travelling, until we Wee begun to feel our feet. What with schemes on hand for a park on the Common and Beacon Hill, a swimming bath, a hospital, a mortuary, a free library, the bridge slepe,and the rectification of the gravedigger's wages, not forgetting that enlendid diplo- matic feet with regard to the Liverpool Water Rill (which will go a long way towards covering • ne Knee:man at least with undying renewn—a gentleman who mewto deterininwl to brie the rice for fame with tin illustrious namesake Philip, of Al AcArlon) we Amy my that we axe pretty well euppliel with matMr for public debate for eome time to come. In the interest of the very important matters, which will tell upon tke future well-being of ehetower,t would ask "Flaccus,. and those that think with him, to defer the agitation in (avow of Sunday traffic to • more eonvenient time; meanwhile the Bradford motto can be . acted goon by all Sunday travellers, for It teguirts A coneAlerable ant Aunt of truiilde to climb lice! bridge steps, bat tabor ono.. Tiwit. I munt ray. however, that Fleeces" has dieplayed in hie style of argu- ment an ingenuity worthy of a b..tter cause, when he quotes Scripture in favour of Sabbath desecration, viz, the parable of the unjust judge. The comparism of Mr. Moon to the unjust judge ir hardly flattering to that renowned railway Official, I shotc,l imegine. I am not one of those people whose air wo are Ao severe As to lead them to my it is a sin to sneeze on a Sunday, yet, without being so strait-laced, should depr,atn an ogita,ion on the question of running Sunday trains from Rnncorn for some time to come. There em few people who would have any need to use the trains if they were put on. animg the first to travel by them would be preAehers and pigeondlyers and err may irately me the former ought not, while the latt. r need not make railway journeye on that day. The only other people who call for consideration are those thirsty souls who walk every Sunday to Frpdsharn Bridge for a pint of beer.a. bona fide trav,llen. The other Sunday morning a hundred pinta of ale were wen at one time on the table of a dirty little beerhouse in that neighbourhood. One is almost inclined to pity them un- fortunate Idiots, and on the ground th it it in not worth the trouble of walking so for to gain en little, offer to help them too ride there and back, so that the doubtful benefit of the pint may not evaporatA before "opening time" at night when they return home. But eeriously, to compare Runcorn with Widnee—that unimmoved second edition of one of the cities of the plain, is had enough, but that the eomparimn should be made out to be unfavourable to Runcorn as regards Sunday behaviour ie a trifle trio good. T.. be sear Widnes station on Sunday evening at traM time, is simply sickening, and if vie are to haven nitnilar scene of rowdyism at the Runcorn station in consequence of Sunday traffic, then I hope the railway authorities vrill keep to their present arran,ement for a long ' time to come. We cannot hope to eucemsfullv resist the encroaching epirit of the age in regard to Sundsiobservmce, but we need not help to hurry forward that spirit of laxity. The Mier course will be to let the thing alone and be ready in the end to accept the inevitable. Even " Pleccus" will admit the °tweet reasonableneas" of such a course.-1 are, sir, yours truly, J. Runcorn, July 20 1880.

STARRING CAMS AT kgmeow.—At the Leigh Petty See- ! Mons, on Monday last, Mn, Thomas Bate, a farmer living at Kenyon, was brought op on a charge of stabbing another farmer named Faulkner. It appeared that the prisoner and prommutor (who are both well-to-do farmers) gnerrelled about three years ago respecting some land which Bate had sub-let to bin neighbour. On Ftiday morning last, as Faulkner, leco npanied ky his son, was reterning home in a trap, he met Bate in a lane leading from the direction of Warrington. Sr...lung wee mid which seemed to have greatly irritated Bute, who broke his walking stick in strik- ing the pr,eetztor, who then seised Bale and pat him on the ground. Faulkner told Bate he did not wish to harm him, promising to release him if he would go quietly home, but Bate declined 10 .10 eo, end set hi. dog on Faulkner, whose tr.., were torn and his log bitten by the animal. While Faolkner Wli endeavoluing to beat off the dog, Bate jumped ap, and deliberately drawing his pocket knife, at- tempted to stab the prosecutor. He struck and inflicted a wound on the left side of the neck, end contienlng the at- tack, /dabbed the man on the left arm in three or four places. l'he right hand was also nut, and he st ibbed him in the ab- domen. Faulkner nacceeded in pitching Bate over the hedge, end, hiss. having called some haymakers, the aff fir waa ended: baton the arrival of the haymakers, it is elated Bate still held the knife In a threatening attitude, saying he would take Faulkner', life. Faulkner irscame exhausted from loss of brood, and Dr. Sephtonwas meedily summoned. It VAR found the knife had prnetrated half an inch into the stomach. Information was given to the police, and Bate was arrested. The prosecutor was stated to be Mill very ill tel could not appear In mart. Thr weather, which was very showery on leaving E trlertown, cleared up during the morning, the sun shining beautifully, end sparkling on the water of the Mersey in the distance, forming an agre,ble contrast to the green fields of grain and other cultivated grounds in front and on the left, acd the rustic little town itself rn the right. ITwe replv to questions front various hon. members, the Marquis of if ARTINOTOSt made a statement in reference to the defeat of General Burrows, at , Candahar. He said he W. happy to state that the tele- graphic messages which he bad received ltd. morning were on the whole of a more reamuring eliaracter—(hear, hear) —and showed, in his opinion, that the statement received yesterdayne to the annihilation of General Burrcom's form I well an exaggeration. Ace convenient form of giving the information to the House, he read a summary of the tele- ' graphic messages which he had received. Before telegraphic ! communication closed at 11 Am. on the 27th, the followiog news was received from Primrose :—.officers of Barrow. 's force who reached Candahar aately, reported to 11 a.m. on , the 27th Colonel Sr. John, Colonel W. Mainwaring. 300 h , Native Infantry; Colonel C. Griffith,, let Native Infantry; Major Oliver, the 66th Foot ; Lieutenant Whittuck, lot Native Infantry ; Lieutenant Umghegan, 3rd Cavalry; Surgeon-Major Harvey, Horse Artillery ; Surgeon Burrows, ! 3rd Scinde Home ; J. Eaton, 16th simive Infantry ; and . A. Dane, Isl Native Infantry; General Big rows, com- I mending the form, and the Wall Slime All Khan have also I arrived at Candahar." General Primrose telegraphed to General Phayre, who is at Chaman about 120 miles from Candahar, just before the wire was cut "I received your telegram of last night. Anxious to me you coining with as large • force as you CAO. Small parties of Burrowsk force ! constantly arriving. It would appear they were pursued ! only three or four miles. Have not vet amen-lined our losses, but fear they have been severe. 'Two guns lost. Have sent Brooke out to assist and bring it, stragglers. They arr very strong in artillery. They hare 35 guns, which they work well. The casualties which hate been reported area, Ifollow E. B. Artilleri, Lieut. E. Osborne, killed, Major , Blackwood ,wounded ; 6dth Foot, Captain Rob,.rts Lieut. Lynch wooed; 3rd Native Cavalry, Captain Mayne and Limt. Reid wounded ; Isl Native Infmay, Lieu. Aslett killed, Lieut.-Colonel Andereon wounded ; 361 h Native In- fantry, Lieut-Colonel Justice, Captain Smith, and Lieut. Cole killed." General' Burrow's force was I composed as I stated yesterday, and its total strength was emimated at about 2Rri. Sir It. Sandeman telegraphs, " Ile can give no distinct information where and when Burrow'. action was fought, and whether Ile attacked or was attacked. Whet] the wire broke l'rimrose did not know the extent ,d the defeat, but that the disaster was not great as at first believed, although very weere. Primpew only fears emrcity of water." The Viceroy telegraph, "Khan of Khelat having heard of Burrow's defeat, lea, telegraphed to Sir It Sandeman expressing his einem° devotion to the British Government, and offers every sasistance in hie power; ptices resources of his State cleat disposal, sending 110 camels and 166 hones at once, and

t I expresses readinem to supply any grain required. I hay< replied expressing cordial appreciation of the Khan's ,! loyalty and promptitude." (" Hear. hear," and cheers.) I The noble Lord concluded ho expressing his fear that , although, as be had said, these reports were more remain, ing, there was no doubt a aevere defeat he been antlered, • and there was reason to fear that this might lead to a prolongation of the war. Under the circum- stances he had thought it necessary, after consultation with the Secretary for War and the Commander-in-Chief, to make arrangements for sending reinforcements of British troops in anticipation of the ordinary relief. In answer to further questions, the noble Ltd said be had no information to give the House as to the preeent state of the defen,s of eAllli4 He would direct • statement of the officers of General Boo- rove'. force to be prepared, together with the information as to those returned to Candaliar, and this should be hung up in I the library. As soon as Burrows's force was moved front Candahar, it WAS decided to send General Phayre with rein- forcementa from Bombay to reinforce the division on that i line. The number of these reinforcements he did not know, ' nor did he know the movements subsequent 0 the desertion of the Web's troops. Lbegraphic oornmuniestion was open with Quettah, but not between QtnUsh and Candahar. He , had received no information of the interruption of telegraphic ""nn'unication with C.,bul. lie had no informal ioo to give astowhat decision had been arrived at with rega rt I to Yakoob Khan and his family, and be did not think it weald hr right at the present time, and in the late,ata of the i.haent A meer, to release a man who could not but be regarled in the light of • rival. _

Hanes AND RAIINITY BILL—On the order of the day for resuming the adjourn..l debate on the second reading of the Harm and Rabbits BiII.--Mr. IiI.ADANOND presented a peti- tion in favour of the bill from 127 larmere of Haddington- shire. (Laughter.)—Lord Ewan presented a petition against the bill from Sir T. Gladstone. (Renewed laughter.) The debate was renamed by Mr. Bruno, who had on the paper the notice of an amendment to the effect that, while the House recognised the necessity of protecting ion legista- lion children and others who could not protect themselves, it Was of opinion that it was not expedient to restrict or in- terfere with the freedom of contract between independent persons of full age aml under Do legal dimbilitv, nor with the use and enjoyment of land as they might am re. The hon. gentleman said if the bill should Oct into committee it Wen INS intention to move an nmendmentdeclaring that hares an,l rabbits should not lie deemed "game" within Hu. meaning of the game lows—Lord LIIdINGTON regarded the poposals of of the bill as a perfectly fair and just settlement of the question.—Sir H. Sabwris lune-mos, oppoeed the bill.— Mr. Howann denied that the farmers, who, ho said, owned fully one-third of the game of the country, could be charged with any desire to ennul.iloreg.,,,eei hut he thought the time had come when the Legislature should put a amp to the sy.tem under which one man Won allowed to feed his game on the proceeds of another man's capital and induetry. The hill, though unanibitious, wan one that met the deo and.. of tha tenant farmers, although lie should have preferrnl giving them the sole right, instead of a right noneurrently with that of the landlords to the ground game. One result of giving the farmers a right to the ground game would lk, that it would stimulate kiln to greater exer- tion in the protection of the winged game, and would greatly aid in the putting down of poaching. The hon. gentleman read letters from agriculturalists, and quoted from the evidence given before the last sel, ct committee on the Game LAWN, with a view of allowing that a vast amount of dentruction was done to the crops tn; ground game, one farmer stating that he had only floraehed 12 quer era of wheat out of a field which ought to mat would have produced a hundred but for its proximity to a wood on which game wee over preserved.—Mr. Hudson, Mr. Patrick. Mr. Gregory. Mr. Pell, and Mr. Heresford Hope, opposed the hill. and Sir A Gordon, Mr. H. Fowler, Mr. Shaw hefeere, and Mr. Arthur Elliot, supported the bill. The house dividnl on Lord John Manners's motion for tlto adjonnunent of the debate. For the motion 118, against 255, majority 137.

SERIOUS CIIAiiE AGAINST A WAR- RINcION 'IRADESSIAN. At the Ifor,:n, pop, sesaiono, on Tuesday last. before rAward Greenell and J. J. Pan, thorge Shone, a greer.groar living in Chorrh-street.Warriegton,woocharted under • remand with Bleating an iron screw lifting jack, value £2, from an engine at Orappenhdt, the property of Wm. Stinker, of Calvelev, near Chester. Mr. Mooreoolicitor, Warringlon,defended the prisoner. William Shelter, the prosecutor, an agricultural engineer. said : On the 2nd July a porbilile Steam engine belonging to etc..,ne Oroppenholl, near the Dog an.l Dart Inn. I was moving it to Warrington, and one of the wheels gave way as we come along. I was therefore obliged to leave it on the : aide of the road at Grappeuhall. I had used a screw lifting jock for Working the engine up, and after finishing with it, I put it into the Mel.e of the engine, and left it there. I did not see the engine again until the 7th hint., when I went to repair it. I found that the screw jock was gone, but nothing else was miming. I gove information I. the police. The sante afternoon, in company with Sergeant !tooth, I went in inspoet the premises of the prisoner in Warrington. , As we were going down the street prisoner asked me if I I should know the screw jack again. I replied, "I should be gleul to we it." Ile said." II td it a handle?" I replied that it had. We examined the prisoner't premises, but found nothing. On the following Monday I received a telegram, in consequence of which I went to the Warrington Police Station. I saw • screw jack there. which let once identified Rs on properly. The handle has been token off also the number on the side. The handle and the number appeared to have been filed off. I produce one aimilar to the one stolen.—Orms-examined by Mr. Moore. I left the boiler and : engine from the 2nd to the Oil, to like care of thetneelves. A Mr. Pemberton, who lives in the neighbourhood, looked after it an well as he could. '•`

James Vernon, a workman in the einploy of rho procreator, said that on the 2nd July he went to lirappenhall to take the wheels off the machine. He identified the screw jack by a small chip on the top. Witness had used it before, and on the day in question, by Mr. Shaker's onlers, he pat it into the firebox. It bad then a handle and a number "3" upon it. Both appeared to have heen since tiled off. The last time witness saw the screw jack safe was on the 3rd net., when be raw it in the firehox. Mary fleece, the wife of Wm. Bleaae, a tanner, resoling at Grappenhall, on the 6th July stn the prison., come along the h ighway la.tween twelve and one o'clock with cart laden with furniture. Witness ran him Irive ep lathe engine and stop, anti afterwards saw him with the fire box door open. She then heard something he ivy dropping into the cart. He then not on his cart and drove away. Gilbert Warburton, a lad living in Church-at., Warring. ton, deposed to finding the screw-jack produced in a ditch at Howley, and afterwards taking it to Messrs. Collins, in Acsdenly-street. Cross-examined I was told to say that the screw-jack produced was the one I found iu the ditch, before I came into court. An extraordinary general meeting of the shareholders of ! Pirr's Banking Company, Limited, was held at the Bank, Winwiclustrect, yearenlay, for the purpose of sanctioning ! the declaration of an interim dividend, and conducting the ordinary busitnes of the company. The chair was occupied hy the chairman, Mr. J. Charlton Parr, and there were also preeent :—Dirretore: Mr. J. Fenton Greene'', I deputy- • chairman); sir Uilbert Greens'', Bart., Sir Thos. U. Frost, Wears. P. stubs, E. Greenall, Thomas Philip Parr, 11. ! Woodcock. N Ectersley, J. Peareon, A. Hewlett,. Cecil F. Parr, George 111cCurqualale, and T. H. Dixon.: Shareholders: Rt. Hon. Sir It. A. Cross, It,. Molyneux, Mess., R. Piernoiet, R. Davies, J. R. Buckton, C. White, C. Broadbent, It. W. Murray, H. Sleekly, 11. Milling, J. Lathgoe, and T. Fairhurst ; John Dun, manager. ; and J. Murray, secretary. Mr. Dux read the report, which was as follows :—The ! directors have load before them the audit balance sheet of ! the bank 0, 30th June, and they beg to report that the profits of the veav•fter providing amply for all bad and doubtful debts, have been satisfactorily. Thedirectorsrecommend that there be now declared for the half.year ending 30011 June, INV. an interim dividend at Bic rate of £IS per rent. per annum, free of income tax, and payable on and after oth August. After providing for this dividend there remains a considerable balvnce, which is writs' forward to next account. The position and prospects of the business con- tinue to he in every way satisfactory:

The Cuonvan: in moving the eidoption of the report, asid lee need trouble them with very few words for, as they all knew, that was an imerim mee,ing foe the declaration of • dividend, and not for publishing the accounts. But he was very happy to tell them that the Liminess, as the report hail it, was in every way satisfactory, and the increase lath in the accounts and in the general turnover Of the bank 19.01 in ev.ry way aatisfactory, and 1113 t another feature which would tied Ideate them was that the la ul debts were inconsiderable in atnnunt and few in number—in fact during these times it perfectly astonished him that they had so few of them. There was one pond that had given them a good etc-al of pun that he felt very aorry to refer to, and Beat was the death of their manager at Chester—Mr. Milner. Ile lead been long associat,al with the lank at Warrington, and as soon ale he had beoee transferreel to Cheater he (flee chairman) believed lie gained the retrain and confidence eel all their friend. and clients in Chester, and he was alni of the greatest assistance, at the time of the tranaler of the businesa, in the carrying throogh of the accounts. NINTH LANCASHIRE RIFLE VOLUNT FESS. This regiment is now undergoing as ann.l tmining in preparation for the annual inspection, which is fixed for to-deY (SatmanY). As. previously reported, last Saturday's parade Mewed • total of 209; Sunday, 211 ; Monday, 389, the latter being one in excess of the corr.. pooling parade List year. On Tuesday a good muster took place. 374 men being on parade. This is th• largest num- ber which has been together on any of the training parades for the past ten years, and must be considered very eatisfactory evidence that the regiment is 5. vigorous as ever. After being " told off " into seven companies, the men marched to Aroley, where a ye, useful drill was gone through, under Colonel &remelt, the commanding officer. The tegirmoll then marched to the Drill Hall, and were dismissed. The officers present were Colonel Greened, Colonel Retrain. Captains Litton, Bolton, Bridge, Lieuts. Elogarth, Hepherd, J. Hepherd, Gooch, Thompson. and Ridgway. On Wednesday the muster was exactly the same as on the corresponding day hot year, namely, 288. Six companies were formsd, arid the drill woe conducted in the field M front of the Town Hall. The bayonet exercise w. perfortned Ins creditable manner, considering the tired state of the men, who, after working all day. had been under arms nearly two !tours when it commenced. The officern were the same as 00 l'uesday. On Thursday the "foil in" sounded at the usual hour, when 372 men answered to the roll out. These were formed irto seven companies of 311 tiles each, and went put through various battalion movements, which occupied two hours, after which the regiment marched to the Drill HAII and was dismissed. List evening the volunteers underwent another inspection. and afterwards partook of refreshments at the Drill Hall. Since the corps was inauguiated 21 years ago it Inte steadily increased in numbers, and to-day, in point of strength snit dficiency, may be said to compare favourably with any other corps in the county. To-day a grand inspection of the corps ik ill take place in Arpley Fields. Yesterday afterno,n the officers id the 9th Lancashire Ride Volunteers gave an "at home " at their head quarters on a moat elaborate scale. The Drill Hall was beautifully decorated. by Meesrs. Eaatero.,l Bros., the celebrated deco- rative arbors, of hfanchester. and the exhaustive embellish- menteof lags, banneretts, Ac, gave it an aspect the most pleasing and delightful. A I.pace of land at the rear of the company's head quarters, unlade empleyed as a drilling area, was occupied with a number' of tents for the purposes of dincing ,tc, and in one corner of the ground, the regi• mental band and an excellent string band under the leader. ship of Mr. T. M. Pattison, discoursed the most lively and interesting music. The pumas began m arrive about three o'clock, and dancing commenced erhortly afterwards.
